name: The Carpenter household
head: carpenter_philo

arrival.note: 'Arrived here in July, 1832' - month precision, stated twice by Andreas in two chapters.

reason_for_coming.note: Not attested. A druggist arriving in July 1832 arrived four months after the Black Hawk War and a month after the cholera; nothing says whether either brought him.

works_at.note: THE TWO-SHOP PROBLEM, INHERITED FROM THE STRUCTURES LAYER. This dataset holds both philo_carpenter_log_shop on Lake Street near the river and carpenter_south_water_store, and Andreas says he removed FROM the first TO the second. The South Water store is the later of the two and is where the sources leave him, so it is the link; the log shop's own record already argues that its survival to the scene date is doubtful. Inferred, because 'subsequently' is not a date.

present_on_scene_date.note: Andreas repeatedly notes him as 'still living in Chicago' in 1883; he is continuous in the record from 1832.

persons.name: Philo Carpenter

occupation.note: 'The earliest pharmaceutist of Chicago was Philo Carpenter, who arrived here in July, 1832, shortly thereafter opening a variety and drug store on what is now known as Lake Street, near the eastern bank of the river; and subsequently removing to South Water Street' (Andreas, scan p. 955). He advertised drugs, medicines, oils, paints and dye-stuffs in the Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833, over copy dated 22 November.

persons.note: DOCUMENTED CONTEMPORANEOUSLY AND RETROSPECTIVELY, which almost nobody in this parcel is. He was one of the twenty-eight electors of 10 August 1833 and got one vote for trustee; he was one of the nine village citizens among the twenty-six founding members of the First Presbyterian Church on 26 June 1833, and one of its three first elders, and Andreas notes he was the only Presbyterian among them, the rest being Congregationalists. Andreas vol. 1, printed p. 132 (scan p. 281), 'an imperfect list of the denizens of the town in the fall of 1833, not before named' - a name, a trade and usually an arrival year, compiled fifty years after the fact. OLD SETTLERS, 1882 — CORROBORATION, NOT A NEW FACT ABOUT 1835. The Calumet Club's fourth annual reception to the settlers of Chicago prior to 1840, held 18 May 1882, printed this man among the guests present as “Carpenter. Philo, 57 Ashland avenue, Chicago.” (Chicago Tribune, 19 May 1882). The club's criterion was residence in Chicago before 1 January 1840 and majority by then: the roster therefore corroborates a pre-1840 Chicago residence and says he was alive in 1882. It gives NO year of arrival, and the address it prints is where he lived in 1882, forty-seven years after the scene date — it is not an 1835 residence and is not read as one. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a later recollection corroborates, enriches and dates and cannot lift a rung by itself, so this record's GRADE IS UNCHANGED by it: T-0513 consolidates the identity and T-0515 regrades. Identity by rule OS1 — surname and spelled-out forename agree, one bearer (data/research/old_settlers/crosswalk.json). THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 3 times: Poll list of the first election of the Board of Trustees of the Town of Chicago, 10 August 1833 — “Carpenter, Philo” (poll_1833_006, line 27); Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Carpenter, Philo” (tax_1833_012, line 64); Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Carpenter, Philo” (poll_1834_023, line 192). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Carpenter' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json).

research_note: CHICAGO'S FIRST DRUGGIST, AND THE HOUSEHOLD THAT SHOWS WHY A RESIDENT CAN OUTLAST A BUILDING LINK. Carpenter is documented from July 1832 to the 1880s; which of his two shops he was standing in on 1 July 1835 is a structures question this project has already argued and not settled.

directories.note: LATER EVIDENCE, BESIDE THE 1835 CLAIMS AND NOT INSIDE THEM. A Chicago directory of 1839, 1843 or 1844 meets somebody of this name and this pass records what it prints. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry.

address_later.note: Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 prints this address against this person, in the entry quoted on the card: 'Carpenter, Philo, druggist and apothecary, South Water st'. It is evidence about 1839, written here as 1839's and read back onto no 1835 claim. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry. The value is the volume's own line, split by its crosswalk on the entry's punctuation. These volumes set the trade first and its qualifiers after it on the same line, so the split may carry an employer, a market or a corner along with the trade. The printed entry is quoted beside the value for exactly that reason: the split is checkable against it, and neither is read into an 1835 claim.

back_projection.note: NOT READ BACK, BECAUSE SOMETHING BETTER ALREADY STANDS. Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 prints an address against this name in 1839, and it is left where it is. An 1835 placement already stands: this household works at `carpenter_south_water_store`, and clause 2 says an attested 1835 placement always beats a door printed 4 years later. The later address stays on the record as 1839's evidence and moves nothing.
